sec.t:
In March 1974, farmers in a village near Xi'an were digging a well during a [[drought|drought]]. They found pieces of clay and a head. [[archaeologist|Archaeologists]] soon realised it was part of something huge.

So far, four main pits have been found. Pit 1, the biggest, is about as long as two football fields and holds rows of infantry soldiers. Pit 2 has archers, cavalry and chariots. Pit 3 seems to be a command post. Pit 4 is empty, perhaps unfinished. Only a part of Pit 1 has been fully dug out.

When new, the army was a riot of colour. Soldiers wore red, green, purple and blue robes, with pink faces and black hair. Among the paints was a human-made [[pigment|pigment]] now called Han purple.

Most of the paint has flaked away underground. When archaeologists dig up a soldier, the remaining paint can curl and fall off within minutes as the damp clay dries in the air. Chinese and German scientists have worked on chemicals to hold the colours in place, but most figures are left grey. That's one reason digging is slow.

The emperor's own tomb lies under a large mound, about 1.5 km from the army pits, and has never been opened. About 100 years after his death, the historian Sima Qian described what was inside. He wrote of palaces, treasure and rivers of mercury that flowed by machinery, guarded by crossbows set to fire at intruders.

Scientists testing the soil above the mound have found unusually high levels of mercury, which suggests Sima Qian's story may hold some truth. Sima Qian also said about 700,000 workers built the complex, though historians think that number may be exaggerated. China has decided not to open the tomb until it can protect what's inside.

Qin Shi Huang united China's warring states, standardised its writing, coins and weights, and linked earlier walls into an early version of the [[@great-wall|Great Wall]]. He was also harsh, ordering books burned and scholars punished. He searched for potions to live forever. Some of those potions may have contained mercury, which possibly harmed him.

He died in 210 BCE, and his [[dynasty|dynasty]] collapsed within four years. His clay army, made of fired [[@terracotta|terracotta]] like Indian pots and temple tiles, has lasted far longer. Today millions visit the site, one of the great discoveries of [[@ancient-china|ancient China]].

text: Slavery in what became the United States began in the early 1600s, when enslaved Africans were brought to the colonies to work on farms and plantations. By 1860, nearly 40 lakh people were enslaved, mostly in the southern states.

It ended through a long struggle. Enslaved people resisted and escaped. Abolitionists, people who wanted to abolish slavery, wrote, spoke and protested. Northern states banned it one by one. Finally, the [[@us-civil-war|Civil War]] of 1861–1865 broke the power of the slave-holding South, and in December 1865 the [[@us-constitution|13th Amendment]] made slavery illegal everywhere in the country.

myth: The Civil War had nothing to do with slavery.

sec.t:
Over about 350 years, roughly 1.25 crore Africans were forced onto ships and carried across the Atlantic Ocean, mostly to the Caribbean and South America. Around 4 lakh were taken directly to North America. In 1619, about 20 Africans arrived in the English colony of Virginia, an early step in a system that grew for generations.

Enslaved people were treated as property. They could be sold, and families were often split apart. Children born to enslaved mothers were enslaved too. In the South, their forced labour grew [[@clothes-cotton|cotton]], tobacco and rice, making plantation owners rich.

Enslaved people resisted in many ways: working slowly, keeping their music and faith, learning to read in secret, and running away. Some escaped north along routes known as the [[@usa-underground-railroad|Underground Railroad]], helped by a hidden network of people. It was not a real railway, but it used railway words: guides were "conductors" and safe houses were "stations". [[@harriet-tubman|Harriet Tubman]] was its most famous conductor.

[[@frederick-douglass|Frederick Douglass]] escaped slavery in Maryland in 1838 and became a powerful speaker and writer. His [[autobiography|autobiography]], published in 1845, showed thousands of readers what slavery was really like. Sojourner Truth, who had walked away from slavery in New York in 1826, travelled the country speaking against both slavery and the unfair treatment of women.

Northern states ended slavery gradually after the Revolution, and importing enslaved people from abroad was banned in 1808. But the South depended on enslaved labour, and as the country grew west, the two sides fought over whether new states would allow it.

In 1852, Harriet Beecher Stowe's novel *Uncle Tom's Cabin* sold hundreds of thousands of copies and turned many northerners against slavery.

When [[@abraham-lincoln|Abraham Lincoln]], who opposed the spread of slavery, was elected in 1860, southern states began leaving the Union. The Civil War followed.

Freedom did not bring equality. The 14th and 15th [[@constitution-amendments|Amendments]] promised citizenship and the vote to Black men, but southern states soon passed laws to keep Black Americans apart and away from the ballot box. Breaking those laws took another century and the [[@civil-rights|civil rights movement]].

Britain's [[empire|empire]] ended most slavery in 1833, but India was left out of that law at first. Slavery was made illegal in British India ten years later, in 1843.

text: On 17 December 1903, Orville Wright flew a wood-and-cloth aeroplane for 12 seconds near Kitty Hawk, North Carolina. It travelled about 37 m, less than the distance from the middle of a cricket ground to its boundary. On 20 July 1969, Neil Armstrong stepped onto the Moon.

The gap between those days was less than 66 years. One person could have watched both, and some did. The leap happened because many problems were solved in quick succession: better engines, metal planes, jets and finally rockets. Two world wars and a race between rival countries poured huge amounts of money and effort into each step.

A feather from a bald eagle
A model of Sputnik

st.reveal: Armstrong carried a scrap of fabric from the Flyer's wing and a piece of its wooden propeller. They had travelled 12 seconds through the air in 1903. In 1969 they made the trip to the Moon and back.

d.try: Make a timeline of flight across a long corridor or garden wall. Use one big step for every five years, starting at 1903. Put sticky notes for the first flight, the first jet, Sputnik and the Moon landing. Then pace out how close together the big moments are.
myth: The Wright brothers were the first people ever to fly.

People had flown in hot-air balloons since 1783 and in gliders before 1900. The Wrights made the first controlled, sustained flight in a powered machine heavier than air. That is what made modern aeroplanes possible.

sec.h: Wood, cloth and a bicycle shop
sec.t:
The [[@wright-brothers|Wright brothers]], Wilbur and Orville, built bicycles in Dayton, Ohio. Their real breakthrough was control. They learned to twist the wings slightly to tilt and steer, much as a bird changes the shape of its wings. They also built their own lightweight engine, because no company could supply one.

That first flight was so short that it would fit inside the wingspan of a Boeing 747. The brothers made three more flights the same day. The longest, with Wilbur at the controls, lasted 59 seconds and covered about 260 m.

Within ten years, planes were crossing seas. Louis Blériot flew across the English Channel in 1909. In 1919, John Alcock and Arthur Brown flew nonstop across the Atlantic. In 1927, Charles Lindbergh did it alone, staying awake for more than 33 hours.

While aeroplanes improved, a few people dreamed of leaving the air altogether. Wings need air to push against, and space has none. Only rockets work there, because they push against their own exhaust.

In 1926, an American physics teacher named Robert Goddard launched the first rocket powered by liquid fuel. It flew for about 2.5 seconds and landed in a cabbage field. Newspapers mocked him, claiming a rocket could not work in empty space. He kept going anyway. During the Second World War, Germany built large military rockets, and after the war both the USA and the Soviet Union hired its rocket engineers.

In 1957 the Soviet Union launched Sputnik, the first satellite. In 1961 it sent Yuri Gagarin into [[orbit|orbit]]. The USA felt it was losing the [[@space-race|space race]], and President John F. Kennedy promised to land Americans on the Moon before 1970.

The rocket built for that job, the Saturn V, stood about 110 m tall, roughly as high as a 36-storey building. Its first stage burned fuel at a rate of about 13 tonnes every second. The flight computer on the Apollo spacecraft had less memory than a modern calculator.

Orville Wright lived until 1948, long enough to see jet planes and a pilot break the speed of sound. On the Moon in 1969, Armstrong carried a scrap of cloth from the Flyer's wing and a sliver of its propeller. Today that first Flyer hangs in the Smithsonian in Washington, D.C., not far from the Apollo 11 capsule that brought the astronauts home.

text: Germany is a country in the middle of Europe, with the Alps in the south, the North and Baltic Seas in the north, and the Rhine flowing through hills dotted with castles. It has more people than any other country in the European Union.

It is known for many things. People think of its cars, engineers and fast motorways, its forests and [[@neuschwanstein|fairy-tale castles]], its bread, sausages and pretzels. It is famous for composers like [[@classical-western|Bach and Beethoven]] and for scientists like Einstein. Its history has some of the darkest chapters of the 20th century, and it is also known for how seriously it has faced them since.

myth: There is no speed limit anywhere on Germany's autobahns.
Many stretches do have speed limits, especially near cities, at junctions and in bad weather. Other stretches have only a recommended top speed of 130 km/h.

sec.t:
In 1812 two brothers, Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm, published a collection of German folk tales. It included Hansel and Gretel, Snow White, Cinderella and Rapunzel. Many of the original versions were much darker than the cartoons you may know. You can trace them in [[@fairy-tales|fairy tales]].

Bringing a decorated evergreen tree indoors at [[@christmas|Christmas]] is a German custom that spread across the world in the 1800s. And in 1840, a teacher named Friedrich Fröbel named his school for young children a "kindergarten", or children's garden, where they learned through play.

In 1886 Karl Benz built a three-wheeled motor car driven by a petrol engine. It is widely called the first true car. His wife, Bertha Benz, drove it about 100 km to visit her mother in 1888, partly to show the world it worked.

Germany's motorways, the autobahns, are famous because some stretches have no fixed speed limit. Germans are also famous for recycling. Shops charge a small deposit on bottles and cans, which is paid back when you return them, so very few end up as litter.

In the 1930s, the [[@holocaust|Nazi party]] under Adolf Hitler took power. It started the [[@world-war-two|Second World War]] in 1939 and murdered about six million Jewish people, along with many others, in the Holocaust. [[@anne-frank|Anne Frank]], whose diary is read around the world, was born in Frankfurt.

After the war, Germany was split. In 1961 East Germany built the Berlin Wall to stop people fleeing to the West. It fell in 1989, as told in [[@berlin-wall|the Berlin Wall]], and Germany reunited in 1990. Today German schools teach this history in detail, and memorials stand in the middle of Berlin.

German scholars studied [[@sanskrit|Sanskrit]] closely in the 1800s. Max Müller, born in Dessau, edited a full printed edition of the Rigveda, and the Goethe-Institut centres in India are called Max Mueller Bhavan in his honour.

Beethoven was born in Bonn in 1770. Albert Einstein was born in Ulm in 1879. Both towns have museums about them, and both men are still among the most famous people Germany has produced.

text: Kolkata sits on the Hooghly River in West Bengal. For more than a century it was the capital of British India and one of the biggest cities in the British Empire. That past left grand buildings, India's first metro and trams that rattled through the streets for 150 years.

But what people love most about Kolkata is its spirit. It is a city of books, poetry, films, football, sweets and long arguments over tea. During Durga Puja, the whole city turns into an open-air art gallery. Today around 1.5 crore people live in its wider metropolitan area.

Nuts and bolts

st.reveal: Workers joined the steel with rivets, metal pins heated until glowing and then hammered flat on both sides. As they cooled they shrank and pulled the plates tight. The bridge opened in 1943 and still carries a huge flow of people and vehicles every day.

sec.h: Three villages and a trading post
sec.t:
In 1690, Job Charnock of the [[@east-india-company|East India Company]] set up a trading post beside three villages: Sutanuti, Gobindapur and Kalikata. The last probably gave the city its name. The British built Fort William and the town grew around it. Calcutta became the capital of British India in 1772.

Merchants, clerks and labourers poured in from across Bengal and beyond. In 1911 the British moved the capital to [[@delhi|Delhi]], but Calcutta stayed India's largest city for decades more. Its name was officially changed to Kolkata in 2001.

In the 1800s, Calcutta became a centre of new thinking, a period later called the [[@bengali-renaissance|Bengali Renaissance]]. Reformers such as Raja [[@raja-ram-mohan-roy|Ram Mohan Roy]] and Ishwar Chandra [[@ishwar-chandra|Vidyasagar]] campaigned for women's education and against cruel customs. Colleges, [[@hist-first-newspaper-india|newspapers]] and printing presses spread new ideas fast.

[[@tagore|Rabindranath Tagore]], born in Kolkata in 1861, became the first Asian to win the Nobel Prize in Literature, in 1913. He wrote the national anthems of both India and [[@bangladesh|Bangladesh]]. Later, the film-maker [[@satyajit-ray-stories|Satyajit Ray]] made films here that are studied around the world, and [[@mother-teresa|Mother Teresa]] ran her mission for the poor in the city.

Every autumn, during [[@durga-puja|Durga Puja]], Kolkata's neighbourhoods build pandals, temporary halls made of bamboo and cloth. Some are shaped like temples, ships or castles. Inside stand clay idols of the goddess Durga, made by craftspeople in the area called Kumartuli. Millions of people walk from pandal to pandal late into the night. In 2021, UNESCO added Durga Puja in Kolkata to its list of the world's intangible cultural heritage.

Kolkata's horse-drawn trams began in 1873 and electric trams in 1902. Only a few routes are left now, but it is the only city in India that still runs them. In 1984, the city opened India's first underground metro. Its yellow Ambassador taxis became a symbol of the city.

Kolkata is also famous for sweets like [[@bengali-food|rosogolla]] and mishti doi, sweet curd set in clay pots. South of the city, the river meets the sea in the Sundarbans, a mangrove forest where tigers swim between islands.

text: Texas is big because of how it joined the United States. It was once part of New Spain and then Mexico. In 1836, settlers there won a war and declared the Republic of Texas, an independent country. Nine years later, in 1845, the USA agreed to take it in as a single state, with all its land at once.

Today Texas covers about 696,000 km², more than a fifth of India's area. Only [[@alaska|Alaska]] is bigger. About 31 million people live there, more than in any state except California. A drive across Texas from east to west can take more than 12 hours.

st.reveal: The 1845 resolution said up to four new states could be formed from Texas, making five in all, if Texas agreed. It never did. Many Texans are proud of their size and have never wanted to divide.

sec.t:
Texans like to say that six flags have flown over their land: Spain, France, Mexico, the Republic of Texas, the Confederate States during the [[@us-civil-war|Civil War]], and the United States. Before any of them, many Native American nations lived there, including the Caddo, Comanche and Apache.

In 1836, a small group of Texan fighters was defeated at the Alamo, an old mission in San Antonio. Weeks later, Texan forces won the Battle of San Jacinto, and Mexico's leader signed away the land. People in Mexico and Texas still tell this history in different ways.

When the USA annexed Texas in 1845, the agreement included an unusual promise. Texas could later divide itself into as many as five states. Texans never used it. In 1850, Texas sold its claims to land further west, now parts of New Mexico, Colorado and other states, for 10 million dollars. Even after that, it stayed huge.

sec.h: From cattle to oil to rockets

sec.t:
Texas has pine forests in the east, flat plains in the north, deserts and mountains in the west, and beaches on the Gulf of Mexico. Big Bend National Park lies on a great bend of the Rio Grande, the river that forms the border with [[@mexico|Mexico]].

The weather can be extreme. Northern Texas gets many [[@tornadoes|tornadoes]]. In 1900, a [[@hurricanes|hurricane]] struck the coastal city of Galveston and killed thousands of people. It is still the deadliest natural disaster in US history.

Texas food mixes Mexican and American cooking. [[@tex-mex|Tex-Mex]] dishes such as fajitas, nachos and chilli con carne are eaten across the USA. [[@bbq|Texas barbecue]] is famous too, with meat smoked slowly for many hours. Large Indian-American communities in Houston and Dallas have added temples, cricket clubs and [[@diwali-lights|Diwali]] celebrations.

Texans are known for being proud of their state. Their flag has a single star, which is why Texas is called the Lone Star State. People there also like to say "everything's bigger in Texas".

text: Animals don't speak in words. A bark or a crow is a noisy mix of sounds that doesn't match any human language. When people try to write it down, they have to squeeze it into the sounds their own language uses.

English speakers hear "woof". Hindi speakers hear "bhau bhau". Japanese speakers hear "wan wan". Spanish speakers hear "guau guau". None of them is wrong. Each is a best guess, shaped by the sounds a child grows up hearing.

Words that copy sounds are called onomatopoeia, from Greek words meaning "making a name". Every language has them, but each one makes them differently. The word itself is famously hard to spell, even for adults.

sec.t:
Each language uses a limited set of sounds. English has the sound "th", which Japanese does not. Hindi has sounds like "bh", which English rarely uses. When a sound copies a bark, it gets built from the pieces each language already has.

Once a word is chosen, it sticks. Children learn it from parents, books and cartoons, and then hear the animal that way. That's why a rooster crows "cock-a-doodle-doo" in English, "kukdoo-koo" in Hindi, "kikeriki" in German, "cocorico" in French and "kokekokko" in Japanese.

Ducks quack in English, go "coin-coin" in French and "gaa gaa" in Japanese. Even cats vary. English cats say "meow", Japanese cats say "nyaa" and Korean cats say "yaong". Pigs oink in English and go "buu buu" in Japanese.

sec.h: Words for things that don't make sounds
sec.t:
Some languages go much further. Japanese has thousands of these sound-picture words. "Doki doki" is a pounding heartbeat. "Kira kira" is the twinkle of something sparkly. "Shiin" is the sound of complete silence. Many are written in a special script, part of [[@japanese-writing|Japanese writing]].

[[@hindi-language|Hindi]] and other Indian languages love doubled sound words too. Rain falls "tip tip", a phone rings "tring tring" and something sizzles "chhan". Many Bollywood songs use them in their lyrics. Children's rhymes in Tamil, Bengali and Marathi are full of them too, because they are fun to say.

[[@comics-art|Comics]] depend on these words. "POW", "BAM" and "WHOOSH" turn silent pictures into noisy action. In Japanese manga, sound words are drawn as part of the picture itself.

Here is the twist. Dogs and roosters sound the same everywhere, but some animals really do have local [[dialect|dialects]].

Many songbirds learn their songs from adults nearby. Over generations, birds in different areas develop slightly different tunes, a little like accents. Scientists have mapped dialects in sparrows across North America, part of the long story of [[@birds-sing|why birds sing]].

Humpback whales in one ocean share a song that slowly changes over time, and whales in different oceans sing differently. Even naked mole rat colonies have their own chirping styles.

So while human words for animals are just guesses, some animals pass down their own sounds as a kind of culture. And the strangest part? Scientists are only beginning to decode what these calls mean, a puzzle at the heart of [[@animal-communication|animal communication]].

text: "Weird" depends on where you grow up. A child in Sweden might find a mango pickle shocking. A child in Gujarat might find a cheese full of blue mould odd. Every country has foods that look strange to outsiders and feel like home to the people who eat them.

Some of the most famous examples are fermented fish that can clear a room, eggs with green yolks, soup made from bird spit and chutney made from ants. Most of them came from clever ways to preserve food, use every part of an animal or find [[protein|protein]] where it was plentiful.

st.prompt: Century eggs, a Chinese delicacy, have dark green yolks and amber jelly-like whites. How long are they really kept before eating?

options.t: A few weeks to a few months

st.reveal: Despite the name, century eggs are usually preserved for weeks or months in a mix of clay, ash, salt and lime. The alkaline mix changes the proteins, turning the white into jelly and the yolk creamy and green.

sec.t:
In the forests of Similipal in Odisha, people of the Mayurbhanj region collect red weaver ants and their eggs from leaf nests in the trees. The ants are ground with salt, ginger, garlic and chilli into a sour, spicy paste called kai chutney. It's said to taste a bit like lemon, because the ants contain an [[acid|acid]].

In January 2024, Similipal kai chutney received a GI tag, a label given to products linked to a special place, like Darjeeling tea. In Chhattisgarh, a similar dish called chaprah is eaten too. Across the [[@northeast-food|Northeast]], people eat silkworm [[pupa|pupae]], crickets and other [[@insects-food|insects]]. The UN's food agency estimates about 2 billion people around the world eat insects.

Century eggs from China are duck or chicken eggs coated in clay, ash, salt and lime for weeks or months. The whites turn into brown, see-through jelly and the yolks turn dark green. They're often served with tofu or rice porridge.

In Southeast Asia, swiftlets build nests from strands of their own [[saliva|saliva]], glued to cave walls. Bird's nest soup has been a luxury in China for centuries. Collecting nests from tall caves can be dangerous work.

On the Italian island of Sardinia, there's casu marzu, a sheep's cheese deliberately left for cheese flies to lay eggs in. The [[larva|larvae]] soften it. Food safety rules in the European Union mean it can't be sold in normal shops.

Disgust probably helped our ancestors avoid rotten food. That's why strong smells hit so hard: your [[@nose-smell|nose]] is checking for danger. But disgust is also learned. Children copy the faces adults make at the dinner table.

Scientists have found that people often start to like a new [[@taste-why|taste]] after trying it many times. Plenty of foods now loved around the world once seemed odd. Raw fish in sushi, blue cheese and even tomatoes were once thought strange or risky by many people. And somewhere in an Odisha forest, a family is enjoying ant chutney made from just a few of the roughly 20 quadrillion [[@ants-world|ants]] scientists estimate live on Earth.

text: It depends on who you ask. To a [[botanist|botanist]], a scientist who studies plants, a fruit is the part of a plant that grows from a flower and holds the seeds. Its job is to help those seeds spread.

"Vegetable" isn't a scientific word at all. It's a cook's word for the other parts of plants we eat: roots, stems, leaves, flowers and bulbs. So in the kitchen, fruits are usually the sweet parts we eat as snacks or dessert, and vegetables are savoury parts we cook into meals. The two lists overlap, which is why tomatoes and brinjals cause so many arguments.

sec.t:
By the botanist's rule, many things we call vegetables are really fruits. Tomatoes, brinjals, bhindi, cucumbers, pumpkins, bottle gourds, bitter gourds, capsicums and [[@chillies|chillies]] all grow from flowers and hold seeds.

The same rule makes some [[@berries|surprising berries]]. A berry, to a scientist, is a fleshy fruit grown from a single ovary with seeds inside. Grapes, [[@guava-papaya|guavas]] and [[@food-why-bananas-curve|bananas]] qualify. Strawberries and raspberries don't. Even the whole pumpkin is a kind of giant berry, botanists say.

Real vegetables come from every other part of the plant. [[@food-why-carrots-orange|Carrots]], radishes and beetroot are roots, which store food underground. Spinach, methi and cabbage are leaves. Onions and garlic are bulbs, made of thick, layered leaves.

Some are trickier. A potato looks like a root but is really a swollen stem, which is why it has "eyes" that sprout shoots, as you can read in [[@potatoes|the potato's story]]. Ginger and [[@turmeric|turmeric]] are underground stems too. Cauliflower and broccoli are tightly packed flower buds. Sugarcane is a stem full of sweet juice.

In 1893, the US Supreme Court was asked whether a tomato was a fruit or a vegetable. It mattered because the USA taxed imported vegetables but not fruit. The judges agreed that botanists call it a fruit, but said that ordinary people cook and serve it as a vegetable, so it should be taxed as one. The full story is in [[@tomatoes|the tomato's tale]].

The ruling shows that both answers can be right. Science sorts plants by how they grow. Kitchens sort them by how they taste and how they are eaten.

sec.h: Why both matter for your plate
sec.t:
Whatever you call them, fruits and vegetables give you [[@vitamins|vitamins]], minerals and fibre, which helps food move through your gut. Different colours often mean different [[@food-nutrients|nutrients]], which is why doctors suggest eating a mix.

India grows more fruit and vegetables than almost any country except China. India's biggest fruit crop is the banana, and its biggest vegetable crop is the potato.
